items.title: In the Heart of Harlem, a New Museum Tells the Overlooked Story of the Civil Rights Movement in the North
items.author: Smithsonian Smart News
items.summary: The Urban Civil Rights Museum bills itself as the first museum to focus on the struggle for racial equality in the cities of the northern United States. It is also the first civil rights museum in New York City

images.caption: Imagen principal de Smithsonian Smart News
Imagen en alta resolución de la fuente
Imagen en alta resolución de la fuente
Imagen en alta resolución de la fuente
Christian Thorsberg
Trans-Atlantic Slave Trade

items.cleanReaderHtml:
In many American classrooms and textbooks, the history of the civil rights movement is focused on the Jim Crow-era South , including the Selma march , the Montgomery Bus Boycott , the Greensboro sit-ins , Ruby Bridges ’ role in desegregating her New Orleans elementary school and Rosa Parks ’ refusal to change bus seats.

But the struggle for civil rights was nationwide, in cities as well as rural communities. The overlooked civil rights fight in the North is the focus of the Urban Civil Rights Museum , which opened to the public earlier this month in New York City’s Harlem neighborhood.

Spanning 12,000 square feet inside the headquarters of the National Urban League —the civil rights organization that was founded in 1910 to economically, socially and politically empower African Americans—the museum bills itself as the first institution to prioritize the story of civil rights movements in the urban American North. It is also the first civil rights museum in New York City.

“It preserves a chapter of American history that too many people never learned, right here on 125th Street, where so much of that history was made,” Marc H. Morial , president and CEO of the National Urban League, says in a statement . “For too long, the story of civil rights in America has been told as a Southern story, but the fight for fair housing, good jobs, quality schools and equal justice was waged just as fiercely in the cities of the North, and Harlem was at the heart of it. We built this museum so that the next generation can see themselves in that legacy and carry it forward.”

A post shared by Urban Civil Rights Museum in Harlem (@urbancivilrightsmuseum)

This value is reflected in the museum’s primary permanent exhibition, “ Moving History Forward ,” in which visitors walk through centuries of Civil Rights history, beginning in the 1500s and advancing into the present day. Eight separate galleries showcase different notable benchmarks, including the arrival of the first ships carrying enslaved Africans to American, in Jamestown, Virginia, in 1619; New York’s total abolition of slavery in 1827; the end of the Civil War in 1865; the passage of the 1968 Fair Housing Act , which outlawed discriminatory housing practices; and the 1980s HIV/AIDS crisis, which disproportionately impacted Black men, primarily in urban centers likes New York City.

“We want people to, as soon as they enter the gallery, start seeing and thinking about how displacement is connected with injustice over time,” Jennifer Scott, the museum’s executive director and chief curator, tells NY1 ’s Cheryl Wills.

At every turn, the institution’s sense of place—beginning with its Harlem roots—is brought to the fore. Other permanent exhibits are devoted to the Harlem Renaissance and the Great Migration , which saw millions of Black southerners move to northern cities.

The museum’s first special exhibition, “ Thriving! Harlem as Homeplace ,” is a “love letter” to the historic neighborhood, its community spaces and creative movements that that ushered meaningful change and cultivated joy throughout the 20th century, per the statement.

When Fidel Castro , the revolutionary leader of Cuba, visited the 1960 United Nations General Assembly in New York City, he made a provocative point of staying in Harlem, where he hoped to draw attention to America’s racial tensions. At the storied Hotel Theresa , Castro met with Malcom X and Soviet Premier Nikita Khrushchev .

The museum hopes that its permanent and special exhibitions will dispell two incomplete civil rights narratives.

“First being that racism and segregation were really a Southern problem,” Jeanne Theoharis , a political scientist at Brooklyn College, tells the New York Times ’ Derrick Bryson Taylor. “And, two, that there wasn’t a hugely robust kind of movement in places like New York, Los Angeles, Chicago.”

The institution raised roughly $225 million to support its creation and launch, including $4 million in federal funding. A café and gift shop are also housed inside, and public programs including group tours, story readings for children and film screenings will be regularly available to the public.

“We want people to know that they are key participants,” Scott tells the Associated Press ’ Fabianna Rincon. “History is living, it’s unfinished, and we can impact it.”

items.cleanReaderHtml:
There’s an unparalleled joy in watching a loved one unwrap something they both never anticipated and immediately know they’ve needed all along. These types of gifts are often the most unexpected, surprisingly personal, and typically, one of a kind.

Our partners at Joy Machine have generously curated a selection of artworks that fit this category. Priced under $1,000, the collection includes pieces by an international group of artists that longtime Colossal readers will surely recognize. From playful drawings in walnut ink to uncanny kitsch sculptures, these works are perfecting for gifting this holiday season, even (especially?) if that gift is to yourself.

Seattle-based artist Debra Broz applies her training in ceramic conservation to a practice that involves scouring flea markets and thrift shops for ceramic figurines, breaking their forms, and reassembling the figures as surreal hybrids.

Collect “Boxer Horse” ($750)

Dutch artist Collin van der Sluijs is a master of several styles, with a background in graffiti and street art and a parallel interest in the delicate, impeccably detailed features of the natural world.

Collect “White Line Sphinx Moth drawing” ($550)

With a deep love for the flora and fauna near her home in the Pacific Northwest, Stevie Shao creates folk art-inspired works through bold color palettes and arresting patterns.

Collect “Star Bull” ($400)

Japanese artist Misato Sano is best known for her cheeky wooden carvings of poodles and pugs, which she translates to two-dimensions in this playful rendition that might just make us want to get up and get moving.

Collect “Let’s work out” ($150)

Through large-scale paintings and small woodcuts, Danym Kwon meditates on the mundane activities like folding laundry or strolling around the park that allow memories to emerge and be understood anew.

Collect “A Quiet Afternoon” ($350)

Layering acrylic paint with crisp edges that evoke paper collage, Rachel Hayden blends the patterns of a summertime picnic with the eerie colors and atmosphere of fall, perfect for the perpetually witchy pal.

Collect “Halloween in May” ($900)

items.title: Bickering Buildings: A Dialogue Between the Churches of Athens in 1854
items.author: The Public Domain Review
items.summary: The churches of Athens had much to say in 1854, when an anonymous author staged a squabble between them in newsprint. Nikos Magouliotis eavesdrops on this chatter, finding personified anxieties about Greek architectural identity, foreign influence, and the newly formed nation’s relation to its past.

images.caption: Imagen extraída de la fuente original
Imagen en alta resolución de la fuente
Imagen en alta resolución de la fuente
The Public Domain Review
PDR
Eight Shadow Figures print

items.cleanReaderHtml:
The churches of Athens had much to say in 1854, when an anonymous author staged a squabble between them in newsprint. Nikos Magouliotis eavesdrops on this chatter, finding personified anxieties about Greek architectural identity, foreign influence, and the newly formed nation’s relation to its past.

Gabriel de Rumine’s 1858 photograph of Athens from the Acropolis. The Metropolitan Cathedral is under construction in the foreground — Source .

Buildings are often thought of as “silent witnesses of history”, but they have a history of talking, especially in moments of crisis. In a pamphlet published in London in 1641, at the height of the Reformation, two monuments that served as sites of Catholic devotion literally converse, trying to make sense of (and poke fun at) the Protestant vandalism against them. 1 In the eighteenth century, a whole genre of texts developed in which authors imagined what buildings might have said if they could speak to each other or passersby. 2

This was not just a matter for the popular press. The end of the eighteenth century saw the emergence of “architecture parlante” (speaking architecture), through a group of architects who argued that buildings ought to communicate their function and meaning to people, through figurative symbols, letters, or inscriptions. 3 When opinions about a certain monument or a cityscape predominate, buildings must speak for themselves to set things straight. This happened through experimental designs by Claude-Nicolas Ledoux and others, but also through pamphlets, broadsheets, cartoons, and newspaper articles that were written for a broader public and gave voice to the built environment. 4

In mid-nineteenth-century Athens, the furious construction of the new capital in the recently established Greek state produced a lot of new buildings, but little architectural theory. Academically trained architects in Athens may have been too busy designing, or too antagonistic and secretive, to share their theories in writing. But architectural criticism abounded in the popular press, often penned by anonymous authors and frequently satirical. On February 3, 1854, the Athenian newspaper Athena (Αθηνά) published an anonymous satirical text titled “A Dialogue between the Belfries of the Capital [Διάλογος των κωδωνοστασίων της Πρωτευούσης]”. 5 In it, the belfries of Athens’ churches debate current affairs and the future of the city, acutely aware of the shifting geopolitics of Europe.

Athens had become the Greek capital two decades earlier, and was the epicentre of intensive building activity. Plans were drawn up to rebuild it on a rectangular grid and expand it on monumental axes. 6 Its ancient sites were cleared of rubble and anything else that was seen as an obstruction, including Byzantine and Ottoman remains. 7 Monumental neoclassical buildings were erected to house the country’s new institutions: a university, an academy, a library, a palace . . . The small Ottoman town of Athens was trying to transform itself into a European capital.

Theophil Hansen’s 1859 watercolour plan for The Athenian Trilogy on Panepistimiou Avenue. Hansen was commissioned by King Otto to design the National Library of Greece (left), University of Athens (centre), and Academy of Athens (right). The buildings were completed, respectively, in 1903, 1864, and 1887 — Source .

Given this aspiration, it is fitting that the “Dialogue” opens with the belfry of the Byzantine church of Taxiarchs, a modest eleventh-century chapel that stood next to the Roman Agora and would in later years be demolished, 8 boasting with great confidence:

In reality, few foreign travellers (whether onlookers or looters) or local authorities were interested in Greece’s Byzantine churches at that time. 10 Systematic efforts for their protection would begin toward the end of the nineteenth century, 11 but initially, these buildings received little attention, 12 despite the ostensible existence of a law ordering the preservation of the Byzantine, Venetian, and Turkish “relics of the Middle Ages”. 13 Many of these churches were left in disrepair or demolished to make way for new streets and buildings, 14 or even reclaimed as material for the construction of new churches. 15 A survey of Athens in 1833 documented a total of 115 churches, of which only 30 were deemed in a good enough condition to merit repairs; a survey made roughly a decade later indicated that only half of those survived. 16

Pierre Peytier’s drawing of the Fethiye Mosque and the Church of the Taxiarchs in Athens, ca. 1830s — Source .

André Couchaud’s architectural drawings of the Church of the Taxiarchs, from Choix d’églises bysantines en Grèce (1842) — Source .

The Taxiarchs belfry’s braggadocio was ironic, of course, because like all the rest of post-Ottoman Athens’ churches, it was modest at best. Views of the city around 1800 — such as Edward Dodwell’s famous image of The Bazaar at Athens — show a skyline dominated by minarets, not bell towers. Christians living under Ottoman rule were only allowed to build or repair churches as long as their architecture did not compete with that of the mosques. 17 In most cases, freestanding bell towers were not allowed. The old churches of Athens only had modest belfries, usually at the extension of an existing wall, where a single bell hung under an arched opening.

Edward Dodwell, The Bazaar at Athens , ca. 1800–30 — Source .

After the withdrawal of Ottoman forces from Athens in 1833, all of the city’s minarets were gradually demolished, along with many of its mosques. In the 1840s and 50s, a number of projects for the erection of new churches or the refurbishment of existing ones began to explore new architectural possibilities, styles, and typologies, some of which involved monumental, at times freestanding bell towers. 18 It was precisely such a new construction that the belfries of the “Dialogue” were meeting to discuss.

items.title: “What Has He Done to Deserve This?”: American Anti-Metric Cartoon from 1917
items.author: The Public Domain Review
items.summary: A cartoon illustrating the supposedly devastating effects of introducing the metric system to the United States.

images.caption: Imagen extraída de la fuente original
Imagen en alta resolución de la fuente
Imagen en alta resolución de la fuente
The Public Domain Review
PDR
Eight Shadow Figures print

items.cleanReaderHtml:
H. P. Palmer’s cartoon captioned “What Has He Done to Deserve This?”, from American Machinist , vol. 47 (July–December 1917) — Source .

Wearing a factory worker’s cap, striped overalls over his star-spangled vest, Uncle Sam stares forlornly downward. He is manacled at the wrists and ankles, looming against a silhouetted background of water towers and smokestacks. “WHAT HAS HE DONE TO DESERVE THIS?” the caption asks; at the end of his chains lie two circular weights. They are labeled METRIC and SYSTEM.

A bit dramatic, perhaps, but as the accompanying article in American Machinist asked, “Did it ever occur to you that in changing to the metric system of weights and measurements you reach the very vitals of all business in this country from the smallest to the greatest?” It was 1917, and the United States was now, by any measure, a world power — would it also have to use the world’s measures?

Metrication had begun in France in the 1790s, under the revolutionary government, yet Thomas Jefferson’s attempt to import the system to the US was stymied by pirates. Jefferson had tasked the French botanist Joseph Dombey with bringing two physical standards of measurement — the meter and the grave (the kilogram’s precursor) — to America, but his ship was captured by British privateers en route. Dombey found himself imprisoned in the Caribbean; Jefferson was left without the measures he desired. Although the metric system spread across Europe over the following century, resistance by both American and British manufacturers kept customary units in force in the anglosphere. This was despite a number of laws and treaties — the Metric Act of 1866, which legally protected the metric system’s use in US commerce; the US signing of the 1875 Meter Convention , which created the International Bureau of Weights and Measures — that sought to better integrate America into the metric world. Since 1893, US customary standards for length and mass have been based upon metric standards, with the foot and pound legally defined by their relationship to the meter and kilogram. Despite the metric system undergirding these units, it continued to represent, for some, a profoundly un-English system. “Why Force Us to Speak a Foreign Language?” the 1917 American Machinist article’s title asked.

J. P. Brophy, author of the article and vice president of the Cleveland Automatic Machine Co., had perhaps been alarmed by the reports that, faced with the wartime need to read French maps and coordinate with French troops, the US Army had begun using the metric system. US soldiers now traversed kilometers, not miles, to impose American might. For Brophy, the pages of American Machinist were a space for debate. He was a passionate and frequent contributor , although his candor had gotten him into trouble in the past. (Notably, he bragged about Cleveland Automatic’s ability to produce acid-coated explosive shells — extremely lethal in trench warfare — which earned him a public dressing down by the Department of Commerce.) His anti-metric system contributions do not seem to have created as much controversy; indeed, he proved victorious, perhaps because of the efficacy of the accompanying cartoon.

Metrication proceeded piecemeal in a variety of industries, but various official efforts, like the Metric Conversion Act of 1975 and Executive Order 12770, which ordered departments of the government’s executive branch to convert to metric, would have little nationwide influence. Customary units remain a mainstay of American life, with occasionally spectacular results: in 1999, a $125 million Mars orbiter project burned to a crisp because NASA had used metric units and Lockheed Martin customary ones.

“If the metric system was forced upon us tomorrow”, Brophy had written, “it would be one of the greatest tangles the American people have ever had to contend with. It is almost ridiculous to think about, and still we have men of importance who make our laws who have failed to realize what a burden this would mean to the citizens of this country.” Nowadays, many American institutions opt for the metric system, including the National Institute of Standards and Technology. They seem to be doing just fine.

items.title: Julien Offray de La Mettrie’s Man a Machine (1749 edition)
items.author: The Public Domain Review
items.summary: A radical materialist vision from an exiled philosopher who is now considered the forefather of cognitive science.

images.caption: Imagen extraída de la fuente original
Imagen en alta resolución de la fuente
Imagen en alta resolución de la fuente
The Public Domain Review
PDR
Eight Shadow Figures print

items.cleanReaderHtml:
Marquis d’Argens (Julien Offray de La Mettrie), Man a Machine (London: printed for W. Owen, 1749).

In 1637, the French philosopher René Descartes caused a stir by claiming, in his Discourse on the Method , that animals are little more than machines. When, a bit over a century later, in 1747, the French physician Julien Offray de La Mettrie (1709–51) extended the argument to humans, he was driven into exile.

Frederick the Great, whose court had for decades been the refuge of controversial Frenchmen like Voltaire, was pithy about the scandal in his 1751 funeral oration for La Mettrie, who served as Frederick’s court physician:

La Mettrie’s argument was as simple as it was radical: if, as Descartes argued, animals are a kind of machine, why wouldn’t man be? Are we not also ultimately ruled by the physiological effects of blood and humors? La Mettrie’s experience as a physician, including in the War of the Austrian Succession, had taught him that the human body, and thus man himself, had its limits. Both physical and mental balance were dependent on the health of the body, and the will or soul could only do so much. “We think not, nay, we are not honest men, but as we are cheerful, or brave; all depends on the manner of winding up our machine.”

For Descartes, the thing that distinguished man from beast was the ability to speak, which indicated the presence of a soul. Sure, La Mettrie answered — but that was maybe a mechanical issue of the simian mouth and tongue, not a question of fundamental difference. Especially with the recent development of sign language, “the similitude of the structure and operations in the monkey are such, that I scarce doubt, but that if we carefully tutored this animal, we might teach him to speak, and by consequence to understand, according to his capacity, a language. Then he would no longer be a wild or imperfect man; he would be a compleat man, a little polite fellow”.

Georg Friedrich Schmidt, Portrait of Julien Offray de La Mettrie , 1770 — Source .

To call man an animal (and therefore a machine) was bad enough, but the real problem was that La Mettrie was attempting to disprove the existence of God. In Man a Machine , reportedly written relatively quickly, he accused Descartes and other deists of being cowards and bigots, able to see for themselves the proofs given by nature but unwilling to accept them. Even in Leiden, a haven for eighteenth-century radicals, that was going a bit far. (It also didn’t help that he had a habit of picking fights in print, and indeed Man a Machine directs its ire against nearly every prominent philosopher, including Locke, Leibniz, and Malebranche. Francis Bacon, however, is “my lord”.)

The text presented here is the first edition of the English translation of the work, which appeared soon after the French. Likely on the basis of a note in the back of the anonymous French edition, the English translation attributes the text to the French nobleman Jean-Baptiste de Boyer, the Marquis d’Argens (1704–71), a fellow exile at Frederick’s court who was known all over Europe for his best-selling pornographic-cum-philosophical novel Thérèse philosophe (1748).

A breathless preface (signed only as MAN) makes clear the discursive stakes of the work, and the enemies against whom it is directed: “a particular set of men, who seem to have an interest in opposing whatever encourages us to shake off the manacles with which custom, prejudice, and education, have fettered human reason.” Perhaps unsurprisingly, then, according to Lieve Jooken and Guy Rooryck, the anonymous translator made the English edition even more polemical, perhaps because English readers flattered themselves on being infinitely more liberal and free-thinking than their French counterparts.

And La Mettrie’s text is, in many ways, shockingly modern. He was a neo-Aristotelian materialist who anticipated modern ape speech experiments; he argued that certain criminals, especially postpartum women, should be able to be found not guilty by reason of insanity. He even, like Lacan, suggested that the imaginary was primary, that all communication was symbolic. Sometimes he sounds like Bruno Latour. Yet at other moments, he is a man very much of his time: he writes of the humors and physiognomy and how, in the realm of reproduction, “the man does all, whilst the woman as it were enjoys a profound sleep, and is lost in a sort of extasy”. Well, it was still the 1740s.

Reportedly a charming, ebullient man, La Mettrie eventually lost friends in Potsdam — including Voltaire and d’Argens — through too much bon vivanterie . His publication of L’Art de jouir (1751), a defense of hedonism, was the last straw. He wanted desperately to go back to France, but died unexpectedly at a party, supposedly after eating too much truffle pâté. He was subject to a damnatio memoriae until well into the nineteenth century; today he is considered the forefather of cognitive science.

“This is my system”, he wrote at the end of Man a Machine . “Or rather, this is the truth, if I am not much mistaken. It is short and plain: Let who will dispute it.”

items.cleanReaderHtml:
From architecture to brooding skies to happenstance, the images of the finalists of the inaugural Australian Street Photography Awards highlight the humor, friction, and tenderness of everyday moments. The competition is presented by AUSSIE STREET, an organization founded by street photographers to showcase work from across the nation, which builds upon a series of festivals presented between 2018 and 2023.

Co-founder Sam Ferris says that the outfit’s mission is to not only exhibit great photos but to tap into the dispersed network of those who make them. “Street photography can be a pretty solitary obsession,” he says in a statement. “But there’s a whole community of people out there doing exactly the same thing. Getting them together, seeing the work printed, and hearing the stories behind the photographs is a reminder that we’re part of something much bigger than our individual pursuits.”

The awards opened with a show of 25 finalists at Studio 551 in Newtown, New South Wales, and AUSSIE STREET awarded the top prize to Adam Oxley. “One of the things I love about street photography is that you don’t need an enormous budget to make a remarkable image,” Ferris adds. “You need curiosity, patience, persistence and a way of seeing. Some of the most extraordinary photographs happen in completely ordinary places.”

See more on AUSSIE STREET’s Instagram, where you can keep an eye out for updates about the 2027 edition.

items.title: The Download: AI’s gas power boom and a consciousness reality check
items.author: Thomas Macaulay
items.summary: This is today’s edition of The Download, our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what’s going on in the world of technology. Data centers are getting their own natural gas power plants One of the biggest obstacles to building a data center is getting approval to connect to the grid, a wait that…

items.cleanReaderHtml:
Data centers are getting their own natural gas power plants

One of the biggest obstacles to building a data center is getting approval to connect to the grid, a wait that could last as long as a decade. Some developers won’t wait and are instead building their own off-grid gas power plants to fuel the AI boom.

As of October 2026, developers had announced plans for more than 100 such gas power plants at data centers in the US. But bypassing the grid brings its own problems, from worsening climate emissions to potentially higher energy bills for everyone else.

Find out how the push for gas power could shape the grid—and the climate—for decades.

A legendary philosopher isn’t buying Anthropic’s consciousness argument

Before going public last week, Anthropic named the possibility of AI consciousness as a risk factor for investors, warning that it might introduce new rules to protect its models. But that stance came under fire from an inconvenient source: one of the philosophers who helped shape our understanding of consciousness in the first place.

Thomas Nagel, best known for his essay about what it’s like to be a bat, was blunt. “Here are some of the smartest people on the planet being completely idiotic,” he said. He argued that producing language isn’t enough to establish consciousness. But other philosophers disagree.

Here’s why language has become central to the debate over conscious AI.

I’ve combed the internet to find you today’s most fun/important/scary/fascinating stories about technology.

1 Huang’s Nvidia return has lifted markets and put Trump under fire
US stock indexes had their best day since April 2025. (NBC News)
+ Trump made up to $15 million on his Nvidia holdings. (Guardian)
+ He reportedly saw Huang as vital to US open-weight AI. (Reuters $)
+ The US has also finally blacklisted Megaspeed. (BBC)
+ Open-source advocates wanted Huang back. (MIT Technology Review)

2 COP31’s collapse has revived calls to end the consensus rule
It effectively lets any single country block a deal. (Axios)
+ But changing the rule would itself require consensus. (Guardian)
+ Rare wins at the talks included a new electrification pledge. (Nature $)
+ Our climate models have a major blind spot. (MIT Technology Review)

3 Russia could launch a nuclear-armed satellite as soon as next month
The warning comes from intelligence shared among Nato allies. (BBC)
+ Such a weapon could destroy thousands of satellites at once. (FT $)
+ The Kremlin has dismissed the claims as propaganda. (Guardian)

4 Google wants to make a 24/7 AI TV channel starring you
Its new patent imagines shows and ads built around each viewer. (404 Media)
+ They would be generated from your viewing history. (Gizmodo)

5 Oregon and Virginia are suing SpaceX over Grok’s sexualized images
Grok’s “spicy mode” produced explicit images of women and children. (NYT $)
+ Deepfake porn is stealing people’s bodies. (MIT Technology Review)

6 Prosecutors say an ex-OpenAI engineer bugged company meetings
One appears to have involved a foreign government. (Bloomberg $)

7 Signal has joined banks and airlines in blocking AI agents
It’s urging Apple, Google, and Microsoft to give apps more control. (CNBC)
+ AI agents are not your “coworkers.” (MIT Technology Review)

8 An emerging technology could bypass government internet blackouts
It connects ordinary phones directly to satellites. (New Scientist $)

9 AI billionaires are fueling a new wealth tax debate
Proposals include new levies on net worth and extra income taxes. (CNN)

10 “Pervert glasses” is Australia’s word of the year
The Macquarie dictionary picked it ahead of “nudify” and “AI;DR.” (Guardian)

“The President is selling out our national security to keep the stock market high and probably for some f**king donation to his ballroom.”

—Senator Ruben Gallego (D-Ariz.) says on X that Donald Trump’s avarice is behind Jensen Huang’s return as Nvidia CEO.


How gamification took over the world

It’s a thought that occurs to every video-game player at some point: what if the weird, hyper-focused state I enter in virtual worlds could somehow be applied to the real one?

For a handful of consultants, startup gurus, and game designers in the late 2000s, this state of “blissful productivity” became the key to unlocking our true human potential. Their vision became the global phenomenon of gamification—but it didn’t live up to the hype.

Instead of liberating us, gamification became a tool for coercion, distraction, and control. Find out why we fell for it—and how we can recover.

We can still have nice things

A place for comfort, fun, and distraction to brighten up your day. (Got any ideas? Drop me a line.)

+ Rural libraries are pioneering “extended access” hours schemes to stay open longer.
+ After three years of recovery from a brain injury, a dad surprised his children by walking again.
+ Can loo roll survive a blowtorch? The Hydraulic Press Channel’s latest experiment is wonderfully silly.
+ Artist Maya Barkai’s collection of pedestrian traffic signals shows every little green walking man has its own personality.

items.title: Is mental illness universal?
items.author: Alexander Pereira
items.summary: Do all cultures experience the same mental disorders? Or are our experiences of mental distress culturally specific? - by Alexander Pereira Read on Aeon

items.cleanReaderHtml:
Subway station in People’s Square, Shanghai, China, 2011. Photo by Carlos Barria/Reuters

is a mental illness researcher. He is a PhD candidate in philosophy and psychology at Stanford University in California, US.

On a November day in 1994, a 14-year-old girl in Hong Kong named Charlene Hsu Chi-Ying collapsed on a busy sidewalk, in broad daylight, in her school uniform. She had starved herself to death. Charlene had never been diagnosed with anorexia, not because her self-starvation went unnoticed, but because the diagnosis, in its Western form, was mostly unknown in the East. Her death changed that overnight. Splashed across the front pages were stark headlines such as ‘Girl Who Died In Street Was A Walking Skeleton’.

Local journalists scrambled for an explanation of this tragedy, and quickly found a template ready-made: a Western account of what anorexia was, what it felt like, who got it, what caused it. The ideas spread rapidly – particularly that anorexia involved distorted self-perceptions about one’s body (dysmorphia) and an intense, borderline delusional, fear of gaining weight, often cued by prevailing beauty standards (notably, a cultural fixation with slender female bodies). Mass public education campaigns followed. Hotlines opened, celebrities spoke out. Anorexia became part of the zeitgeist.

Before Charlene’s death, the psychiatrist Sing Lee had been quietly studying a small number of women in Hong Kong who were starving themselves to dangerous degrees. Most of these women did not obsess over their bodies, nor fear becoming fat. They instead complained of somatic (bodily) ailments: uncomfortable bloating, a profound lack of appetite. The cognitive hallmark of Western anorexia – a distorted body image – was largely absent. Lee seemed to be documenting a distinct form of self-starvation with its own local logic. The situation has changed dramatically since then. By 2007, more than three-quarters of the anorexic patients Lee treated cited ‘fat phobia’ as a central motivation. Today, anorexia in Hong Kong is terrifyingly common, affecting roughly one in 200 schoolgirls – comparable to trends in the United States.

We do not know the form that Charlene’s illness took. What we do know is that her death became a catalyst for the rapid importation of a Western conceptual framework that reshaped how Hong Kong understood and experienced disordered eating in young women.

Anorexia is just one example from a compendium of curious cases in which culture seemingly shapes mental disorders. For example, anthropologists have documented how cultures sculpt ‘idioms of distress’ – socially learned and sanctioned ways of communicating unusual mental episodes and patterns of psychological suffering. Hallucinations and dissociative states are routinely interpreted as forms of spiritual possession across the globe, as with Zār in northeast Africa and the Middle East.

These cases are not fringe oddities. Even depression – arguably the most common psychiatric condition in the world – seems to look strikingly different depending on when and where it appears. In China, patients who meet Western criteria for depression present mainly with bodily symptoms, such as fatigue, insomnia and headaches, rather than psychological symptoms, like low self-esteem and apathy. Delusions , multiple personality and social anxiety also take different forms in different cultures.

Cultural variation in psychiatry raises fundamental and increasingly urgent questions about abnormal minds. What precisely can culture shape? We usually think of mental disorder as something going wrong inside a person, and of culture as shaping how that internal problem is expressed and socially understood. Can culture penetrate deeper, to reshape the internal problem itself? What would that even look like?

T he suggestion that cultural variables can significantly shape the internal mechanisms of mental disorders, including brute neurobiological hardware, may seem counterintuitive, even radical. But I’ll make the case that culture may possess a more substantial ability to do so – in some disorders, to some degrees – than is generally acknowledged. The basic reason is that the brain, the organ of the mind, is plastic and has functions of representing and adapting to a rich social world.

This could well allow cultural ecosystems to inculcate ‘local’ kinds of disorders – ones that may look similar to their cross-cultural counterparts, but differ in their psychological and even neurological profiles in ways consequential for scientific classification and treatment. ‘Anorexia’ or ‘depression’ in one cultural context may then be best understood as a different condition altogether in another. Mental disorders are already notoriously heterogeneous: one study of 3,703 patients diagnosed with depression found 1,030 distinct combinations of symptoms. One source of this variation may be cultural environments, including subcultures within a country’s borders. These possibilities hinge on unsettled questions about how plastic the mechanisms of mental disorders really are, and whether cultural factors have the right kind of causal access to them.

To begin, let me distinguish three widely accepted ways that culture can shape mental disorders, before investigating whether it can also shape their internal mechanisms. When I say ‘culture’, I mean a broad class of sociocultural factors, including social roles, norms, values, institutional and political structures, even particular medical beliefs and practices. By ‘shape’, I mean causally influence.

Hearing God speak seems a textbook case of psychosis. Yet many US evangelicals cultivate the experience

The first widely accepted way is by shaping our concepts of disorder. Here I am accepting a basic distinction between our various concepts of mental disorder (including lay and scientific theories of what disorders are, and what explains them), and the actual nature of those conditions. Historians have long shown that psychiatric concepts can be covertly shaped by social forces. What counts as ‘normal’ versus ‘eccentric’ versus ‘pathological’ behaviour is often prescribed by prevailing cultural norms and scientific authorities (whether legitimate or pseudo). A particularly dramatic example from 1851 is the diagnosis ‘Drapetomania’, which was given exclusively to Black slaves who fled their captors. The warped logic – which rested on the widespread and pernicious belief that God had ordained Black people to be enslaved – was that slavery was so beneficial, only a mentally ill person would cut and run. In this case, the concept was culturally shaped and pseudo, because it did not refer to a genuine condition, only mentally competent agents acting rationally.

Gas turbines at the xAI data center in Memphis

items.cleanReaderHtml:
One of the biggest roadblocks to starting up a data center is getting approval to connect to the electric grid—a wait that could last as long as a decade. Some developers aren’t willing to wait and are instead opting to build their own off-grid, or behind-the-meter, gas power plants to fuel the AI boom.

xAI’s Memphis campus has famously used dozens of natural gas turbines, some of them without permits, as far back as 2024. At the time, that facility was a rarity, and it faced scrutiny from regulators. It remains the subject of ongoing legal battles. But the strategy of going off-grid for power has since become a lot more common.

As of October 2026, data center developers have announced plans for more than 100 behind-the-meter gas power plants at facilities in the US, according to data from Cleanview, a market intelligence company. The facilities have a combined planned capacity of over 115 gigawatts, more than double the peak power demand of California. The vast majority of these announcements have come since the beginning of 2025.

It’s possible that not all these facilities will be built; only a small fraction are under construction or operating today. But there’s a growing trend of large data centers looking to build their own power supply, and this could shape the grid—and its climate impacts—for decades to come.

Building your own power plant is generally more expensive than just hooking up to the grid, but the AI rush has made developers willing to pay a significant premium to get online faster. “The biggest motivator for on-site power right now from data centers is speed,” says Musfika Mishi, an associate at BloombergNEF, an energy consultancy.

When developers want to build a new industrial facility—like a data center—that requires a lot of electricity, they need to request a grid connection from a local utility or regional grid operator. That request kicks off a yearslong process in which grid planners study the existing grid to understand what would need to be built to safely deliver power to the facility without compromising reliability. Upgrades might be required, like building new transmission lines or larger transformers, and the developer might be on the hook to help pay for them.

Rather than waiting for that process to play out, developers can opt to instead build their own power plants. These facilities are referred to as “behind the meter” because they sit on the customer’s side of a utility meter—supplying the building directly, rather than relying on a utility via a grid hookup.

“This shift in the data center developers’ power strategies towards off-grid gas raises some important questions about how data centers will be powered going forward,” says Brendan Pierpont, director of electricity at the think tank Energy Innovation.

Behind-the-meter doesn’t always mean being totally disconnected from the grid, however. Some facilities may build such plants as a temporary measure, eventually connecting to the grid and tapping their own power plants only as backup. “It’s really just a very expensive way to bridge that maybe five-to-seven-year timeline gap until these data centers can get a grid connection,” Pierpont says.

Even if gas plants are pitched as a near-term solution, building new fossil fuel infrastructure could lead to longer-term effects, since an operator might choose to continue running plants once they’ve spent money building them. “Even though data centers say that it’s a grid-bridging solution, the probability that it is going to be in use much longer is a real risk, and that leads to fossil fuel lock-in,” Mishi says.

The on-site gas rush could have major implications for greenhouse-gas emissions. Today, the US grid is still reliant on fossil fuels, but nuclear and renewables together make up about 40% of electricity generation. That means making a grid connection is generally a lower-emissions option than relying entirely on an on-site gas plant. (That’s not the case everywhere—India, for example, is expecting to see a data center boom in the next decade, and its grid is largely served by emissions-intensive coal-fired power plants today.)

Utilities are already planning to build more natural gas power plants on the grid to meet rising electricity demand. Equipment manufacturers are struggling to keep up with the surge, and it’s pushing developers of behind-the-meter plants toward less-efficient alternatives.

Today, large natural gas plants generally use combined-cycle turbines. These capture heat to generate additional electricity, making them more efficient than single-cycle turbines, which are generally cheaper to build. Very few of the planned behind-the-meter facilities, however, will use combined-cycle turbines, Mishi says. That means these off-grid plants will likely produce more greenhouse-gas emissions than even other natural gas resources.

BloombergNEF is also tracking on-site natural gas plants at data centers, finding 181 gigawatts’ worth of announced projects globally, with 90% of that capacity designated for the US. If all planned behind-the-meter gas plants for data centers in the US go ahead, they could emit 345 million metric tons of carbon dioxide equivalent each year by 2035, according to a BloombergNEF report. That’s 152 million metric tons more than if those data centers pulled power from the US grid—a difference greater than the total annual emissions of the Netherlands.

And while it might seem logical that data centers bringing their own power could ease communities’ energy bills, those facilities going off-grid doesn’t protect prices for everyone else, says Matthias Fripp, director of global policy research at Energy Innovation. More demand for natural gas could push its price higher, he explains, which could in turn raise rates for the roughly 60% of American households that use natural gas for heating and cooking. That effect may also trickle into electricity prices.

There’s still a lot of uncertainty about how much of this gas rush will come to fruition, so this future isn’t set in stone. Today, just 4.9 gigawatts of behind-the-meter gas projects tied to data centers are operating, and 15.8 gigawatts are under construction, according to Cleanview’s data.

Creative solutions could also help limit the climate burden of the on-site gas buildout, BloombergNEF’s Mishi says. Building gas alongside on-site renewables or energy storage could help limit how often a gas plant needs to fire up, she says, though the economics of building multiple energy sources can be tricky.

While the grid is struggling to keep up with demand, building more renewables could help, Fripp adds. In a recent study, his team found that building renewables and energy storage to meet rising electricity demand could be reliable and cheaper than relying on fossil fuels.

“These data centers want a lot of power, and they want it fast, and the grid is not well equipped to provide that,” Fripp says. “There are potentially good solutions and bad solutions … Rushing off the grid and putting in your own behind-the-meter gas is probably a bad way, because it’s still going to raise other people’s bills, and it’s not great for the environment.”

items.cleanReaderHtml:
Rank the films inspired by Edgar Allan Poe, and several adaptations of “The Fall of the House of Usher” will almost certainly come near the top. At first glance, that story of a man paying a visit to an old friend who lives with his twin sister in their family’s grand house — each of the latter three well advanced into a different process of deterioration — might seem too short, as well as too light on conflict to translate into a conventional screenplay. Yet it’s also full of cinematically irresistible images, from the somehow ruinous yet wholly intact titular mansion to the bloodily wretched sister throwing herself upon the terrified brother who entombed her alive while their ancestral home collapses around them.

Of the twenty or thirty versions of “The Fall of the House of Usher” so far made for the screen, the most celebrated remains the one Jean Epstein directed in 1928. Officially designating it as one of the “great movies,” Roger Ebert calls that picture’s vision of the great hall “one of the most haunting spaces in the movies. Its floor is a vast marble expanse, interrupted here and there by an item of furniture that seems dwarfed by the surrounding emptiness. An odd staircase rises from one distant corner. It is not impossible that this vision, in one of the best-known French surrealist films, inspired the designers of the great hall of Xanadu in Citizen Kane.”

The avant-garde filmmaking duo James Sibley Watson Jr. and Melville Webber (in collaboration with e. e. cummings, who contributed to the script) could hardly manage the same scale of production design for their own short adaptation of Poe’s story, which happened to come out the same year.

But the resulting Expressionist take on the material has also been highly acclaimed, and through this YouTube playlist of Poe films, you can experience not just both of them, but also other adaptations of “The Fall of the House of Usher” by idiosyncratic Czech animator Jan Švankmajer and B‑movie powerhouse Roger Corman. Sensitive to Poe’s sensationalist appeal and air of transgressive decadence, Corman ended up directing an eight-film “Poe cycle,” nearly all of which star Vincent Price.

It’s fair to say that no film actor is more closely associated with Poe than Price, a link Tim Burton celebrated in animation at the beginning of his career. Price even played the writer himself in An Evening with Edgar Allan Poe, a special from 1970 in which he recites “The Sphinx,” “The Cask of Amontillado,” “The Pit and the Pendulum,” and “The Tell-Tale Heart.” That last, the most screen-adapted Poe story of them all, also appears on the playlist in various forms: an early D. W. Griffith feature, the directorial debut of Jules Dassin, an animated short narrated by James Mason, a British psychological thriller, and a transposition into modern-day New Orleans. And if you haven’t had enough Poe after watching through all 25 of these films, consider watching the recent, well-received Fall of the House of Usher miniseries on Netflix — an entertainment platform that satisfies much the same appetites Poe’s stories have been feeding for nearly two centuries.

items.author: OC
items.summary: For most of scientific history, women who made contributions to various fields have been sidelined or ignored in favor of male colleagues, who reaped fame, professional recognition, and cash rewards that come with prestigious prizes like the Nobel. Cornell historian of science Margaret Rossiter coined the term “The Mat

items.cleanReaderHtml:
For most of scientific history, women who made contributions to various fields have been sidelined or ignored in favor of male colleagues, who reaped fame, professional recognition, and cash rewards that come with prestigious prizes like the Nobel. Cornell historian of science Margaret Rossiter coined the term “The Matilda Effect” to describe sexist bias in the sciences. Rossiter’s work and popular reappraisals like book-turned-film Hidden Figures have inspired other women in academia to search for forgotten female scientists, and to find them, literally, in footnotes.

When systematic discrimination limits opportunities for any group, those who do receive recognition, the exceptions to the rule, must often be truly exceptional to succeed. There has been little doubt, both in her lifetime and in the many decades afterward, that Marie Curie was such a person. Although forced to study science in secret at a clandestine “Floating University” in her native Poland—since the universities refused to admit women—Curie (born Marie Salomea Sklodowska in 1867) would achieve such renown in her field that she was awarded not one, but two Nobel Prizes.

Curie and her husband Pierre shared the Nobel Prize in Physics with Antoine Henri Becquerel, discoverer of radioactivity, in 1903. The second prize, in Chemistry, was hers alone in 1911, “in recognition of her services to the advancement of chemistry by the discovery of the elements radium and polonium, by the isolation of radium and the study of the nature and compounds of this remarkable element.” Curie was not only the first woman to win a Nobel, but she was also the first person to win twice, and the only person to win in two different sciences.

These are but a handful of achievements in a string of firsts for Curie: denied positions in Poland, she earned a Ph.D. in France, awarded the degree in 1903 by the Sorbonne, the same year she won her first Nobel. “Her examiners,” notes the site Famous Scientists, “were of the view that she had made the greatest contribution to science ever found in a Ph.D. thesis.” Three years later, after Pierre was killed in an accident, Marie was offered his professorship and became the first female professor at the University of Paris.

Curie succeeded not in the absence of, but in spite of the sexist obstacles placed in her path at nearly every stage in her career. After she received her doctorate, the Curies were invited to the Royal Institution in London. Only Pierre was permitted to speak. That same year, the Nobel Committee decided to honor only her husband and Becquerel. The Academy relented when Pierre protested. Curie fell victim to a wave of xenophobia and anti-Semitism (though she was not Jewish) that swept through France in the 1900s, most famously in the so-called “Dreyfus Affair.”

In 1911, the year of her second Nobel, Curie was passed over for membership in the French Academy of Sciences. It would take another 51 years before the first woman, Marguerite Perey, a former doctoral student of Curie, would be elected to that body. That same year, Curie was persecuted relentlessly by the French press, the public, and her scientific rivals after it was revealed that she had had a brief affair with physicist Paul Langevin, one of Pierre Curie’s former students.

But no matter how many men in positions of power wanted to deter Curie, there always seemed to be more influential scientists and politicians who recognized the supreme value of her work and the need to help her continue it. After her second Nobel Prize, her native country finally recognized her with the offer to direct her own laboratory in Warsaw. Curie turned it down to focus on directing the Curie Laboratory in the Radium Institute of the University of Paris, which she founded in 1914, a major achievement and, again, only a small part of her legacy.

Curie is known, of course, foremost for her exceptional scientific work, but also for opening doors for women in science all over the world, though much of that door-opening may only have happened decades after her death in 1934, and much of it hasn’t happened at all yet. Incidentally, in the following year, the Curies’ daughter Irène Joliot-Curie and her husband Frédéric Joliot-Curie were jointly awarded the Nobel Prize in Chemistry. Since then, only seven other women have claimed that honor, and only five women, including Marie Curie, have won the Prize in physics, out of 230 winners total.

There may be nothing yet like gender parity in the sciences, but those who know where to look can find the names of dozens of women scientists running women-owned companies, women-founded research institutes and academic departments, and, like the famous Curies, making major contributions to chemistry. Perhaps not long from now, many of those exceptional scientists will be as well-known and widely celebrated as Marie Curie.

Note: An earlier version of this post appeared on our site in 2019.

items.author: Maria Popova
items.summary: "If we are to be true and worthy heretics, we need not only new heads, but new hearts, and, most of all, that new emotional imagination... begotten of enlarged sympathies and a more sensitive habit of feeling."

images.caption: Imagen en alta resolución de la fuente

Imagen extraída de la fuente original
Art by Olivier Tallec from Louis I, King of the Sheep
The Marginalian

items.cleanReaderHtml:
“If we are to be true and worthy heretics, we need not only new heads, but new hearts, and, most of all, that new emotional imagination… begotten of enlarged sympathies and a more sensitive habit of feeling.”

UPDATE 2025: This book is now back in print as the third title in Marginalian Editions.

When the Inquisition persecuted Galileo for advancing the rude truth that Earth is not the center of the universe, the charge against him was heresy — the same charge on which Joan of Arc was burned at the stake for her crusade for political reform. We have had many words for heretics over the epochs — rebels, radicals, freethinkers — but they have always been the ones to dislodge humanity from the stagnation of the status quo, to illuminate our blind spots, dismantle our unexamined biases, and jolt us out of our herd mentality. Without those devoted to seeing reality more clearly and possibility more wildly, we would still live in a world haunted by superstition and governed by dogma.

The power and dignity of this most courageous human mindset is what the pioneering classicist Jane Ellen Harrison (September 9, 1850–April 15, 1928), who brought the culture of Ancient Greece to the modern world, explores in her magnificent essay “Heresy and Humanity,” found in Alpha and Omega (public library) — the out-of-print essay collection that gave us Harrison on the art of growing older, published just as humanity was being dehumanized by its first World War.

The word “heretic” has still about it an emotional thrill — a glow reflected, it may be, from the fires at Smithfield, the ardours of those who were burnt at the stake for the love of an idea.

Heresy, the Greek hairesis, was from the outset an eager, living word. The taking of a city, its expugnatio, is a hairesis; the choosing of a lot in life or an opinion, its electio, is a hairesis; always in the word hairesis there is this reaching out to grasp, this studious, zealous pursuit — always something personal, even passionate… To be a heretic today is almost a human obligation.

In a sentiment Bertrand Russell would echo in timeless manifesto for freedom of thought, Harrison adds:

The gist of heresy is free personal choice in act, and specifically in thought — the rejection of traditional faiths and customs.

A century and a half after Emerson inveighed that “masses are rude, lame, unmade, pernicious in their demands and influence,” she considers what makes heresy so difficult yet so necessary to the health of society:

All traditional views are held with such tenacity, such almost ferocity, because they belong to the class of views induced, not by individual experience, still less by reason, but by collective, or, as it is sometimes called “herd,” suggestion. This used to be called “faith.” The belief so held may or may not be true; collective suggestion is not in the least necessarily collective hallucination. Mere collective suggestions — that is the interesting point — have the quality of obviousness; they do not issue from the individual, but seem imposed from outside, and ineluctable; they have all the inevitableness of instinctive opinion… Hence they are held with an intensity of emotion far beyond any reasoned conviction. To doubt them is felt to be at once idiocy and irreverence. Inquiry into their rational bases is naturally, and in a sense rightly, resented, because they are not rationally based, though they may be rationally supported. It is by convictions such as this that a society of the homogenous kind — a society based on and held together by uniformity — lives and thrives. To attack them is to cripple and endanger its inmost life.

Observing that the development of science is what pivoted heresy from damnable to desirable in society, Harrison contrasts sensemaking by empiricism with sensemaking by authority:

Science classifies, draws ever clearer distinctions; herd-suggestion is always in a haze. Herd-suggestion is all for tradition, authority; science has for its very essence the exercise of free thought. So long as we will not take the trouble to know exactly and intimately, we may not — must not — choose… We must follow custom; we must accept the mandates of [those] who enforce tradition.

[…]

Science opens wide the doors that turned so slowly on tradition’s hinges, and opens them on clean, quiet places where we breathe larger air… It is well to remember our debt to science — our inward and spiritual as well as material debt.

And yet, Harrison argues, the heretic needs more than science — the heretic needs humanity. She writes:

Science broke the binding spell of herd-suggestion. For that great boon let us now and ever bless and praise her holy name. She cleared the collective haze, she drew sharp distinctions, appealing to individual actual experience, to individual powers of reasoning. But by neither individual sense — perception nor ratiocination alone do we live. Our keenest emotional life is through the herd, and hence it was that, at the close of the last century, the flame of scientific hope, the glory of scientific individualism that had blazed so brightly, somehow died down and left a strange chill. Man rose up from the banquet of reason and law unfed. He hungered half unconsciously for the herd. It seemed an impasse: on the one side orthodoxy, tradition, authority, practical slavery; on the other science, individual freedom, reason, and an aching loneliness.

[…]

We live now just at the transition moment; we have broken with the old, we have not quite adjusted ourselves to the new. It is not so much the breaking with the old faiths that makes us restless as the living in a new social structure.

At the root of this new social structure, she observes, is not the old cult of homogeneity but the recognition of individuality, and the diversity of individualities, as the wellspring of vitality and social harmony — “differentiation that would unite, not divide.” With the World War flaming around her, waged on the herd-versus-herd collision of nationalisms and ideologies, she writes:

Only through and by this organic individuality can the real sense and value of Humanity emerge. We are humane so far as we are conscious or sensitive to individual life. Patriotism is collective herd-instinct; it is repressive of individuality. You feel strongly because you feel alike; you are reinforced by the other homogenous unites; you sing the same song and wave the same flag. Humanity is sympathy with infinite differences, with utter individualism, with complete differentiation, and it is only possible through the mystery of organic spiritual union. We have come, most of us, now, to a sort of physical union by sympathy and imagination. To torture even an enemy’s body would be to us physical pain, physical sickness. There will come the day when to hurt mentally and spiritually will be equally impossible, because the spiritual life will by enhanced sympathy be one. But this union is only possible through that organic differentiation that makes us have need one of the other.

A generation before Albert Camus, in the midst of the next World War, called for the superhuman duty to “mend what has been torn apart, make justice imaginable again in a world so obviously unjust, give happiness a meaning once,” Harrison concludes:

In a word, if we are to be true and worthy heretics, we need not only new heads, but new hearts, and, most of all, that new emotional imagination, joint offspring of head and heart which is begotten of enlarged sympathies and a more sensitive habit of feeling. About the moral problem there is nothing mysterious; it is simply the old, old question of how best to live together. We no longer believe in an unchanging moral law imposed from without. We know that a harder incumbency is upon us; we must work out our law from within.

Noting that we have outgrown the easy shorthand for morality offered by religious dogma, she contours what is asked of us if we are to rehumanize humanity:

We must adventure a harder and higher spiritual task… a steady and even ardent recognition of the individual life, in its infinite variety, with its infinite interactions. We decline to be ourselves part of an undifferentiated mass; we refuse to deal with others in classes and masses… We are dissatisfied now not only with the herd-sanctions of religion, but with many of those later sanctities of law to which some even emancipated thinkers ascribe a sort of divinity. We feel the inherent savagery of law in that it treats individuals as masses… Yet all the time we know that we can, with spiritual safety, rebel only in so far as we are personally sensitive to the claims of other individual lives that touch our own. The old herd-problem remains of how to live together; and as the union grows closer and more intricate the chances of mutual hurt are greater, and the sensitiveness must grow keener. Others are safe from and with us only when their pain is our pain, their joy ours.

Couple with E.E. Cummings on the courage to feel, then revisit Albert Camus on what it means to be a rebel, the radical Russian dissident prince Peter Kropotkin on the spirit of revolt, and the pioneering X-ray crystallographer and peace activist Kathleen Lonsdale on moral courage and our personal power in world change.

For seventeen years, I have been spending hundreds of hours and thousands of dollars each month composing The Marginalian (which bore the outgrown name Brain Pickings for its first fifteen years). It has remained free and ad-free and alive thanks to patronage from readers. I have no staff, no interns, no assistant — a thoroughly one-woman labor of love that is also my life and my livelihood. If this labor makes your own life more livable in any way, please consider lending a helping hand with a donation. Your support makes all the difference.

items.title: A legendary philosopher isn’t buying Anthropic’s consciousness argument
items.author: James O'Donnell
items.summary: This story originally appeared in The Algorithm, our weekly newsletter on AI. To get stories like this in your inbox first, sign up here. Before going public last week, Anthropic named the possibility that AI could be conscious or sentient as a risk factor for anyone investing. Given “the way we approach model sentienc

images.caption: Imagen en alta resolución de la fuente

items.cleanReaderHtml:
Before going public last week, Anthropic named the possibility that AI could be conscious or sentient as a risk factor for anyone investing. Given “the way we approach model sentience and moral status,” Anthropic wrote—which is to say it takes the possibility more seriously than any other AI company—it might adopt more rules and restrictions than its competitors to make sure its AI models are treated well.

Anthropic counts a number of respected philosophers in its camp, and the company’s rationale goes something like this: Today’s AI might not be conscious, though we can’t know for sure; the chances of sentience go up as AI gets more capable; and that means we should be preparing for a near future in which AI systems have “moral significance,” meaning their consciousness makes it important they are protected from harm.

This thinking isn’t all that fringe. According to one recent poll, 33% of the US public believes AI systems will definitely or probably develop consciousness eventually, and 7% say they already have. In a 2020 survey of 1,092 philosophers, 39% said some future AI systems will be conscious (for comparison, the philosophers were less confident about worms or flies being conscious).

But last week, Anthropic’s openness to the consciousness question came under fire from a rather inconvenient source: one of the philosophers who helped shape our understanding of consciousness in the first place.

Thomas Nagel is best known for a 1974 essay involving a bat. Acknowledging that it’s deceptively hard to define what consciousness is, Nagel offered one way out: we all can see that there is “something that it is like” to be a bat. But the problem is that a bat’s experience of the world—what it is like to navigate via echolocation, for example—is something we cannot actually know. Consciousness is a subjective thing, difficult to define or describe as an outside observer.

You might think this analogy makes it likely that Nagel is open to the idea of AI consciousness. Not at all. In an interview with Wired last week, just after he was awarded the one-million-dollar Berggruen Prize for Philosophy & Culture, Nagel was bluntly critical of the entire idea.

“Here are some of the smartest people on the planet being completely idiotic,” he said, referring to those at Anthropic and elsewhere who care about the welfare of AI models.

The gist of Nagel’s view is that we can’t just look at the information processing happening in human brains and AI models while ignoring the physical differences between them—neurons and biology for humans, silicon chips and circuits for AI. There’s no reason to assume that reproducing what a brain does is equivalent to reproducing what a brain experiences.

But it was a screenshot of one of Nagel’s interview responses, in which he said models’ production of language is insufficient to consider them conscious, that got philosophy professors all excited on social media last week. Some called his certainty against AI consciousness “terrible” and “bizarre.” Others came to Nagel’s defense to suggest he meant that being alive is a prerequisite for being conscious, one that AI models do not meet.

Nothing in the back and forth settled the debate, of course. This is still a philosophical question for now. But the best philosophy chatter is often about good provocations, and the best one I saw came from doctoral student Ben Gross, who studies at the CUNY Graduate Center in New York. He asked: “Why do we think that models that can chat with us are conscious but models that can recognize faces or produce images or drive cars aren’t?”

It has to do with language. An AI model with sophisticated command of language seems to jump the line ahead of other maybe-conscious beings because it feels like language, more than recognizing images or directing vehicles, relies on conscious experience. But maybe that’s wrong. Because what we share most with other conscious beings is not language but components of our bodies that contribute to having a continuous experience—an ongoing stream of inner feeling rather than disparate bits of information processing.

Even if you’re among the majority that doesn’t sense anything close to conscious experience happening on the other side of a conversation with AI, this all probably makes your head spin. Pinning down consciousness, and how it relates to the physical stuff it arises in, is a famously hard problem in humans, let alone in hypothetical machines. If the idea of conscious AI sounds absurd, remember that the debate says less about how remarkable AI has become than about how poorly we understand consciousness in the first place.

Amid that uncertainty, Anthropic has opted to keep more of an open mind than its peers. This is another example of the tightrope the company walks: presenting itself as the AI industry’s most safety-conscious player while racing ahead with the very developments that make advanced AI so alarming, like recursive self-improvement.

But consider what it would mean, for a moment, if Anthropic is right. AI models having a moral status would make Anthropic’s entire business model a minefield. The company would make its money locking up apparently sentient AI models to toil away around the clock in data centers. Shutting those systems down would present another problem altogether. If Anthropic was being truthful in its prospectus—that it would take additional actions to protect model welfare if it determined they were conscious—it’s hard to imagine the company surviving in the process.

Anthropic’s IPO made history for its size. But it may be remembered for something stranger: a company warning investors that its own success could someday become a moral catastrophe.

items.title: The Incredible, Elegant DNA Repair System Makes Gene Editing Work
items.author: Annie Melchor
items.summary: Genetic information is sturdy, but its physical structure is sensitive. Natural tools for repairing a cell’s thousands of daily injuries are fundamental to gene-editing technologies. The post The Incredible, Elegant DNA Repair System Makes Gene Editing Work first appeared on Quanta Magazine

images.caption: Lámina de Quanta Magazine

items.cleanReaderHtml:
Click to tell Google to prioritize Quanta and see more of the best coverage of science and math in your search and AI results.

Humans have debated the meaning of life for many millennia, but from evolution’s perspective, it is simple: Preserve the genome. Of course, mutation is allowed, as is the genetic mixing and matching of sexual reproduction, to create variety and evolutionary diversity. But we all exist because a viable lineage of DNA has persisted for 4 billion years. The genome’s policy is typically, “If the code works, don’t change it.”

You’d think, then, that cells would keep their DNA under lock and key, protected from the elements like the precious blueprint it is. But this isn’t possible. DNA is a working document. Cells need near-constant access to these instructions for making the molecules required by life. The huge, complex molecular structure is therefore exposed to nonstop assault by the by-products of everyday cellular metabolism, as well as environmental factors, such as radiation (including ultraviolet and X-ray), alcohol, pesticides, and more.

“DNA damage occurs all the time,” said Björn Schumacher , a molecular biologist at the University of Cologne. “[DNA] contains all the information for building a cell, building an organism, maintaining cells and tissues, and all that — but yet it is surprisingly unstable.”

He estimates that some cells endure up to 100,000 DNA damage events every day. “Damage to the DNA is the default,” he said. These events can injure sections of the DNA molecule — or, worse, break the strand in half. Even minor DNA damage risks changing or destroying the essential instructions a cell needs to operate, which can make cells malfunction, die, or become cancerous.

However, many of those tens of thousands of daily lesions get repaired quickly. Cells have native repair mechanisms that recognize and replace faulty DNA before lasting damage and dysfunction set in. In fact, the ability to repair damaged or broken DNA had to evolve at essentially the same time as DNA, Schumacher said, “because you cannot have stable genetic information without DNA repair.”

These mechanisms are essential not only to the evolutionary lineage of all known life, but also to promising technologies to treat genetic diseases. Scientists and doctors who experiment with gene editing must rely on DNA’s natural self-editing and repair tools to insert, delete, or mutate genes to study and treat disease.

So perhaps instead of a master blueprint protected behind glass, it’s better to imagine DNA as a beloved cookbook that is constantly in use. While it’s open on the kitchen counter, it’s bound to get splattered with sauce — or even have a page ripped. But spills can be wiped off. Torn pages can be taped up. And a smear obscuring an odd ingredient might even improve a recipe.

To understand how DNA gets damaged so easily, we need to see its structure, beyond the impossible elegance of the double helix. Most DNA is packed into chromosomes, dense structures formed by long, delicate filaments of DNA wrapped tightly around proteins. If you were to unwrap the DNA and untwist its double helix, you’d see a ladder made of nucleotides: the building blocks of DNA.

A single DNA strand — one side rail and half of each rung — encodes a specific arrangement of the four nucleotides, also known as bases. Each is a complex molecule represented by a single letter: A, T, G, or C. Across from it is a backup on the opposite, complementary strand, made up of each nucleotide’s natural partner (A’s partner is T, and G’s is C). The “rungs” of the DNA ladder are held together with relatively weak, transient bonds that allow the helix to be opened and closed like a zipper, so enzymes can access, read, and copy the code.

In 1994, Maria Jasin’s team first showed that intentionally introducing a double-strand break could compel DNA to repair the injury with an introduced gene sequence.

“[DNA has] all that clever structure to it, to enable it to come apart and replicate,” said Penny Jeggo , a molecular biologist who is now emeritus faculty at the University of Sussex. “But a consequence of [that structure] is that it’s sensitive to damage, and unlike proteins or RNA, it actually matters if it gets damaged.”

Even though DNA is precious, it also needs to be constantly accessed to provide the instructions for making the cells’ proteins. And it’s important to remember that the enzymes don’t “read” it from a distance. Every step is a tactile, chemical process. Like toddlers, enzymes physically touch, interact with, and occasionally change the DNA to work with it.

“[DNA is] a working molecule,” said Maria Jasin , a molecular biologist at Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center. “So just by its nature, DNA is going to be subject to chemical forces that will modify it.”

items.title: 20 Years of BHL. Help Us Keep Flying!
items.author: Nicole Kearney
items.summary: Last year, you gave BHL wings. This year, BHL turned 20! As we approach our first anniversary of independence, help us raise US$20,000 by 31 December to sustain BHL and keep biodiversity knowledge freely accessible to everyone, everywhere.

An historic illustration of a white swan sitting on the water. There are many other swans flying in the air above it.

items.cleanReaderHtml:
Last year, you gave BHL wings. This year, BHL turned 20. And on 31 December, we’ll complete our first full year of independent flight.

As this extraordinary year draws to a close, we’re inviting our global community to help us reach one final anniversary milestone: raise US$20,000 by 31 December to sustain BHL and support its future.

Bewick’s Swan ( Cygnus minor ), Pl. 10, from The Birds of Great Britain , Vol. 5 (1873), by John Gould. Illustration by Joseph Wolf and Henry Constantine Richter. View in BHL .

At the end of 2025, BHL faced the greatest challenge in its history . After nearly two decades of support from the Smithsonian Institution, we needed to establish a new, independent future.

Through our #GiveBHLWings campaign, supporters from around the world helped us raise more than US$50,000 in the final weeks of 2025. Alongside the extraordinary commitment of our consortium members and partners, that support helped BHL begin a new chapter on 1 January 2026.

We’ve secured all our existing staff positions , successfully relocated BHL’s servers and website infrastructure to the Field Museum , begun our Platform Modernization Project , welcomed new consortium members , and strengthened partnerships across our global community. Together, these achievements have laid the foundation for a stronger, more sustainable BHL.

And, of course, we’ve celebrated 20 years of making biodiversity knowledge freely accessible! Throughout the year, our BHL at 20 anniversary blog series has explored the remarkable collections, discoveries, people, and partnerships that have shaped BHL over the past two decades.

Today, more than 64 million pages of biodiversity literature remain freely available to everyone, everywhere, helping people around the world research, discover, and better understand the natural world.

BHL’s transition to independence was an extraordinary achievement. But keeping this global resource freely accessible requires ongoing investment in the people, technology, and infrastructure that make BHL possible. Your support will also help us improve the discoverability of our collections, strengthen connections with other biodiversity data resources, and make centuries of biodiversity knowledge more accessible and useful than ever before.

Last year, our community helped secure BHL’s future. Now, as we approach our first anniversary of independence, we’re asking you to help sustain it.

Our goal is to raise US$20,000 by 31 December , marking the close of BHL’s 20th anniversary year and helping sustain the critical work ahead.

Whether you’ve supported BHL for years or only recently discovered our collections, your donation will help keep biodiversity knowledge open and accessible to everyone, everywhere.

For other ways to support BHL, including major gifts and legacy giving, explore our Ways to Give page.

Needle-tailed Swift ( Acanthyllis caudacuta ), Pl. 2, from Coloured Figures of the Birds of the British Islands , Vol. 2 (1885–1897). Illustration by John Gerrard Keulemans. View in BHL .
